stages.name: Nationalisation: fiscal cost
stages.title: Nationalisation: fiscal cost
stages.sub: Understand why taking a firm into state ownership costs the government money, and what that spending gives up elsewhere.

steps.q: The government takes a private rail company into state ownership. The former owners lose their firm. Would they walk away with nothing, or expect to be paid for it?
steps.right: They would expect to be paid for it
steps.wrong: They would walk away with nothing
steps.hint: It was their private property before. Would the state simply take it for free?
steps.pre: So the government usually has to pay the owners

steps.q: Once the state owns the rail company, wages, maintenance and new trains still have to be paid for every year. Does ownership end the spending, or does it continue?
steps.right: It continues, and the state now pays it
steps.wrong: It ends once the state takes over
steps.hint: Trains do not run themselves. Who pays the staff and upkeep now?
steps.pre: So the state also faces the ongoing

steps.q: Add together the payment to former owners and the yearly running expenses. Is this a one-off bill, or a lasting drain on government funds?
steps.right: A lasting drain on government funds
steps.wrong: A one-off bill that is soon over
steps.hint: One of the two costs happens every year, not just once.

steps.q: The government has a fixed budget. If billions go on compensating owners and running the rail company, can that same money also be spent on hospitals or schools, using opportunity cost thinking?
steps.right: No, that spending is now given up
steps.wrong: Yes, it can still be spent on both
steps.hint: The budget is limited. What happens to other spending once this money is committed?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Weighing up the compensation, the ongoing running costs, and the spending given up elsewhere, is nationalisation financially costless for the government, or a real burden on its budget?
steps.right: A real burden on its budget
steps.hint: Think about all three costs together, not just the initial payment.
